lead: A wide band-gap device is a power switch made from a semiconductor with a large energy gap between its valence and conduction bands. Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) are the two common ones. The wide gap gives a high critical electric field, so a thin drift layer can block high voltage. That means lower on-resistance and faster switching than silicon at the same rating. You meet these devices in electric-vehicle chargers, solar inverters and server power supplies.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for MOSFET behaviour and Chapter 1.7 for gate drive.

blocks.text: The bandgap E_g is the energy needed to lift an electron from the valence band to the conduction band. It is measured in electron volts (eV). One eV is the energy an electron gains when it crosses a potential of 1 volt. Silicon has E_g = 1.1 eV. SiC has 3.2 eV and GaN has 3.4 eV. A wider gap means the material can withstand a stronger electric field before avalanche breakdown. That limit is the critical electric field E_c, in megavolts per centimetre (MV/cm). Silicon breaks down near 0.3 MV/cm. SiC reaches about 2.2 MV/cm and GaN about 3.0 MV/cm.

blocks.where: t_drift is drift layer thickness in cm; V_B is blocking voltage in V; E_c is critical field in V/cm. A higher E_c gives a thinner drift layer for the same V_B.

blocks.text: A thinner drift layer has less resistance when the device is on. Heat also leaves SiC easily because its thermal conductivity is about two to three times that of silicon. GaN conducts heat less well, so it is often grown on a SiC or silicon substrate. The figure plots E_c against E_g for the three materials.

The SiC MOSFET looks like a silicon power MOSFET but uses a vertical structure. Current flows from drain at the bottom to source at the top through a drift region. It is normally off: zero gate voltage blocks. Turn-on gate voltage is often +15 V to +18 V; a negative bias of a few volts holds it off safely. The gate oxide is thin, so the gate voltage must never exceed the datasheet absolute maximum. A SiC MOSFET has a body diode. That diode can conduct in the reverse direction, but it has reverse recovery charge Q_rr.

The GaN HEMT (high electron mobility transistor) is lateral: source, gate and drain sit on the top surface. A thin AlGaN layer on GaN creates a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) — a sheet of mobile electrons with high mobility. Most power GaN HEMTs are enhancement-mode, normally off. The gate window is narrow, often 0 to 6 V, and a spike above the limit destroys the gate. GaN has no p-n body diode. When the source-to-drain voltage reverses, the channel conducts in reverse with a higher drop than a diode. Do not assume GaN has a simple body diode.

items: Read these datasheet lines: V_GS absolute max; R_DS(on) at 25 °C and 125 °C; Q_g; C_oss; R_thJC.

blocks.text: Both SiC and GaN are unipolar: only majority carriers conduct. There is no minority-carrier storage, so turn-off is fast and Q_g is small. Gate drive loss is P_gate = Q_g × V_GS × f_sw, where Q_g is gate charge in coulombs, V_GS gate voltage in volts and f_sw switching frequency in hertz. A small Q_g lets you switch at 100 kHz or more with little drive loss. The penalty is a fast dv/dt — rate of change of voltage, often tens of volts per nanosecond. Fast dv/dt charges parasitic capacitances and causes ringing, EMI and false turn-on. Layout and gate resistors matter.

At 600 V, GaN competes with silicon superjunction MOSFETs. At 1200 V, SiC MOSFETs are common because silicon is lossy and slow. A SiC MOSFET can replace an IGBT in a solar inverter and switch at higher frequency, shrinking the inductor. GaN is used in laptop chargers and 48 V server supplies. Only a few universities teach this at device level.

figure.caption: Each point is a material: silicon at 1.1 eV and 0.3 MV/cm, SiC at 3.2 eV and 2.2 MV/cm, GaN at 3.4 eV and 3.0 MV/cm. Notice that the wide-gap materials sit far above silicon in critical field.

spec.aria: Plot of critical electric field against bandgap for silicon, SiC and GaN, showing silicon near 0.3 MV/cm and the wide-bandgap materials above 2 MV/cm.

examples.question: A SiC MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ. A silicon MOSFET of the same voltage rating has R_DS(on) = 100 mΩ. Both carry a drain current of 20 A. (a) Find the conduction loss in each. (b) Find the ratio P_Si / P_SiC. (c) State one reason to choose SiC.
steps: Conduction loss is P = I² R_DS(on).
Ratio: P_Si / P_SiC = 40 W / 8 W = 5, so P_Si : P_SiC = 5 : 1.
Reason: SiC has lower conduction loss and can switch at higher frequency because it is unipolar with low Q_g.
examples.answer: P_SiC = 8 W, P_Si = 40 W, ratio P_Si/P_SiC = 5; SiC gives lower conduction loss and faster switching.
examples.check:
R_sic = 20e-3
R_si = 100e-3
I = 20
P_sic = I**2 * R_sic
P_si = I**2 * R_si
print(P_sic)
print(P_si)
print(P_si / P_sic)

traps: Wide band-gap devices are not drop-in replacements. A SiC MOSFET may need +15 V and negative off-bias; a GaN HEMT may accept only 6 V. Check the datasheet absolute maximum before power-up.
Do not assume GaN has a simple body diode. Reverse conduction is through the channel, with a higher drop and no Q_rr in the silicon sense.
Fast dv/dt can destroy a device even when average current and voltage look safe. Probe gate-source ringing; add a gate resistor and tighten the layout.
R_DS(on) rises with temperature. Use the hot value, not the 25 °C value, for loss calculations.
Reverse recovery of a SiC MOSFET body diode still exists. It is smaller than a silicon PiN diode but not zero; it can cause losses and ringing.

quiz.q: Define bandgap and give its value for Si, SiC and GaN.
quiz.a: Bandgap E_g is the energy needed to move an electron from the valence band to the conduction band. Si: 1.1 eV; SiC: 3.2 eV; GaN: 3.4 eV.

quiz.q: Why does a higher critical electric field allow a thinner drift layer for the same blocking voltage?
quiz.a: The drift layer must hold the blocking voltage. A material with higher E_c can hold the same voltage across a thinner layer, because thickness is roughly 2V_B/E_c.

quiz.q: A GaN HEMT has Q_g = 8 nC and is driven at V_GS = 5 V, f_sw = 200 kHz. Find the gate drive power.
A SiC MOSFET switches 400 V in 10 ns. Find dv/dt. Why can this cause EMI?
quiz.a: dv/dt = 400 V / 10 ns = 40 V/ns. Fast dv/dt pushes current through parasitic capacitances, causing ringing and EMI.

quiz.q: What is a 2DEG in a GaN HEMT?
quiz.a: A two-dimensional electron gas: a thin sheet of mobile electrons formed at the AlGaN/GaN interface. It is the conductive channel.

quiz.q: Why is a GaN HEMT called a lateral device and a SiC MOSFET vertical? Give one consequence.
quiz.a: GaN has source, gate and drain on the top surface, so current flows sideways. SiC has drain at the bottom and source at the top, so current flows vertically. Vertical devices handle high voltage and heat better.

quiz.q: A SiC MOSFET has R_DS(on) = 25 mΩ at 25 °C and 40 mΩ at 125 °C. It carries 15 A. Find the conduction loss at both temperatures.
A designer replaces a silicon MOSFET with a GaN HEMT and keeps the same gate drive. The GaN gate fails. Give two likely reasons.
quiz.a: The gate voltage may exceed the GaN limit, often 6 V. A negative spike or ringing from the old gate drive and layout can also break the thin gate.

beyond: Not for the exam. SiC and GaN are moving from niche to mainstream: 800 V electric-vehicle traction inverters use SiC, and GaN is common in fast chargers. Search for trench SiC MOSFET, GaN cascode and dynamic R_DS(on) to see current research. Datasheet parameters such as Q_rr and C_oss are the next things to study.
